newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Shares, dollar hit by Wall Street worries.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Shares, dollar hit by Wall Street worries.

text.p: Renewed concern that Wall Street's record-breaking run could be faltering hit share prices around the world on Wednesday and depressed the dollar.

Reviving fears of the red ink that washed over markets late last week, the New York stock wxchange, the world's biggest, opened with pronounced losses as expected. But it then recovered some lost ground on cautious bargain-hunting.

Having been down nearly 100 points or around 1.5 percent within 20 minutes of the opening, the Dow Jones industrial average of U.S. blue-chip share prices recovered to show a loss of around 60 points after an hour.
European stock markets also revived from their lows.

Dealers said concern that Japanese investors might reduce their holdings of U.S. stocks and bonds had applied pressure and raised a question mark over recent strength in top shares, particularly technology stocks.
"People are looking for an excuse to sell," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management in New York. "Investors are extremely nervous."

Wall Street was also jolted by rumours that computer giant IBM was about to issue a profits warning. An IBM spokesman declined comment on the rumours but said the group had no plans for a news release on Wednesday.

A column in the Wall Street Journal had prompted jitters in Asian and European markets, well before New York opened, questioning whether Japanese financial institutions were losing interest in U.S. Treasuries. This also sent bond prices lower.

Concern that Japanese and other investors could trim their holdings of U.S. assets also undermined market sentiment for the dollar, analysts said. In addition, the U.S. currency was jolted by a widening of Japan's trade surplus with the United States.
The FTSE 100 index of blue-chip stocks in London, Europe's leading stock market, lost more than 70 points at one stage but by mid-afternoon showed a drop of around 50, or 1.2 percent.
French and German shares fell up to two percent earlier, amid investor concern that Wall Street might be facing a major correction, but then trimmed their losses to around 1.5 percent.

In two days of recovery in share prices on Monday and Tuesday, stock markets had clawed their way back from sharp losses at the end of last week that followed remarks by U.S. central bank chief Alan Greenspan on the "irrational exuberance" of Wall Street.

U.S. prices at the wholesale level provided relatively few shocks. The November producer price index rose 0.4 percent, matching October's increase, but the core rate, excluding the volatile food and energy sectors, rose 0.1 percent after a 0.3 percent drop in October.
"Its a good core number. That is what the market will be looking at," said Raphael Marrone, money market economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

In other news, the Bank of England signalled no change in official interest rates on Wednesday after a monthly monetary policy meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George.
CURRENCIES AT 1530 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 112.95 yen and 1.5425 marks against 113.29 and 1.5539 in late European business on Tuesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1530 GMT
The FTSE 100 index of leading British shares was 50.0 points lower at 3,985.7.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt ended bourse floor trade down 49.95 at 2,841.05 and was around the same level in mid-afternoon computerised trading.
In Paris, the CAC-40 share index was down 29.06 at 2,222.34.
In Asian trading, Tokyo's Nikkei 225 closed 253.74 points lower at 20,568.38, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index fell 152.86 points to 13,189.60.
PRECIOUS METALS

Gold was fixed back at $368.25 an ounce in the afternoon, unchanged from the previous London close, after earlier rising to around $370. Selling on New York's Comex market contributed to the reversal. Silver edged back to $4.79 versus $4.81.
